metrics.label: P/E (TTM)
metrics.description: Price over trailing twelve-month earnings. Null when earnings are negative — a negative P/E would sort as the cheapest stock on the page.
metrics.usage:
Read the percentile, not the number. 'Under 15 is cheap' is folklore — what matters is where this sits in the stock's own range.

Beware the cyclical trap: P/E is at its LOWEST near a cycle peak, because earnings peak there. A semiconductor or energy name that looks cheap on P/E may be at the point of maximum risk. For those, lead with EV/EBITDA.

metrics.label: EV/EBITDA
metrics.description: Enterprise value over EBITDA. Neutral to capital structure, so it compares companies with different debt loads — which P/E cannot.
metrics.usage:
The multiple to use when comparing companies with different debt loads, or one company across time as its leverage changes.

Always read it next to Net Debt/EBITDA. A low EV/EBITDA on heavy leverage is the classic value trap — cheap because the balance sheet may not survive a downturn, not because the market is wrong.

metrics.label: EV/Sales
metrics.description: The fallback when earnings are negative or noisy. The only multiple that still works on a pre-profit company.
metrics.usage:
Only meaningful alongside gross margin. 10x sales at an 80% gross margin is a completely different business from 10x at 30% — the first can grow into the multiple, the second mostly cannot.

Use it when earnings are negative or too noisy to trust, and treat a high reading as a growth requirement: the company has to deliver years of it before the multiple makes sense.

metrics.label: EV/FCF
metrics.description: Enterprise value over free cash flow. Harder to manipulate than any earnings-based multiple.
metrics.usage:
The most trustworthy multiple here, because cash is far harder to massage than earnings.

Compare it to EV/EBITDA. A wide gap between the two means heavy capex or working-capital drag that EBITDA is quietly hiding.

metrics.label: FCF Yield
metrics.description: Free cash flow over market cap. The one valuation metric directly comparable to something outside the stock market, like a Treasury yield.
metrics.usage:
Set this against the 10-year Treasury. If a mature, low-growth business yields less than a risk-free bond, you are paying entirely for growth that has to actually arrive.

A very high yield is rarely a free lunch — above roughly 8% the market is usually pricing in decline. The question is whether you disagree.

metrics.label: P/S
metrics.description: Price over trailing sales.
metrics.usage: Same use as EV/Sales, but it ignores debt. Prefer EV/Sales whenever leverage is material; P/S is mainly useful for net-cash companies where the two nearly agree.

metrics.label: P/B
metrics.description: Price over book value. Primary for banks and asset-heavy businesses, close to meaningless for asset-light software.
metrics.usage:
Genuinely useful for banks, insurers and heavy industry, where book value approximates what the company owns. Below 1.0 on a bank means the market doubts the stated asset values.

Close to meaningless for software: book value excludes the brand, the code and the people that actually generate the returns.

metrics.label: Revenue Growth YoY
metrics.description: Growth in trailing-twelve-month revenue against a year earlier. The input that justifies any multiple.
metrics.usage:
Watch the trend, not the level. Decelerating growth at a high multiple is the most reliable way to lose money in this market — the multiple compresses at the same time earnings disappoint.

For cyclicals, read it backwards: peak growth is a warning, not a signal.

metrics.label: Gross Margin
metrics.description: Separates genuine software economics from reselling hardware.
metrics.usage:
The clearest read on business-model quality and the hardest line to fake. Rising means pricing power or a better mix; falling means competition or input costs.

For anything marketed as an 'AI' company, this is the tell: real software economics run 70%+, while reselling someone else's hardware runs far lower however the revenue growth looks.

metrics.label: Operating Margin
metrics.description: EBIT over revenue. The spread against gross margin is where operating leverage shows up.
metrics.usage:
Read the gap between this and gross margin — that gap is operating expense. A widening gap on flat gross margin means the company is buying its growth.

Direction matters far more than level, and levels are only comparable within an industry.

metrics.label: Net Margin
metrics.description: Net income over revenue.
metrics.usage: Distorted by one-off charges, tax rates and interest. Use it as a sanity check on P/E, but judge the business itself on operating margin.

metrics.label: FCF Margin
metrics.description: Free cash flow over revenue — how much of a sale becomes cash.
metrics.usage: How much of each dollar of sales becomes cash you could actually take out. The gap against net margin is capex and working capital — a persistent gap means the business needs feeding to stand still.

metrics.label: ROIC
metrics.description: Return on invested capital. Neutral to capital structure, unlike ROE, which leverage and buybacks inflate. Compare against cost of capital: growth only creates value above it.
metrics.usage:
The real test of whether growth is worth anything. Compare against cost of capital, roughly 8-10% for most companies.

Above it, growth compounds value. Below it, growth destroys value no matter how fast the top line moves. A business earning 30% ROIC and reinvesting heavily is close to the best thing you can own.

metrics.label: ROE
metrics.description: Return on equity. Flattered by leverage and buybacks — a company that buys back stock until book equity nears zero shows an absurd ROE. Prefer ROIC.
metrics.usage:
Treat with suspicion. Leverage and buybacks both inflate it, so a heavily indebted company can post a spectacular ROE while earning poor returns on the capital it actually employs.

Companies that have bought back stock until book equity approaches zero produce absurd or negative readings that mean nothing. Use ROIC instead, except for banks where ROE is the industry standard.

metrics.label: FCF Conversion
metrics.description: Free cash flow over net income. The earnings-quality tripwire: sustained readings below ~0.8 mean reported profit isn't becoming cash.
metrics.usage:
The earnings-quality tripwire. One weak quarter is noise; below ~0.8 for several consecutive quarters means reported profit isn't turning into cash.

When it does, look at receivables, inventory and capitalised costs — that is usually where the difference is sitting. Sustained above 1.0 is the mark of a genuinely cash-generative model.

metrics.label: Inventory Days
metrics.description: Inventory over daily cost of revenue. The classic semiconductor cycle tell — inventory building faster than revenue precedes a downturn.
metrics.usage:
The semiconductor cycle's earliest warning, and the reason it sits in that group's profile. Inventory turns over before earnings do.

A sharp rise while revenue growth is flattening is the classic pre-downturn signature: product has stopped moving, but the income statement hasn't admitted it yet.

metrics.label: Diluted Shares
metrics.description: Share count over time. Dilution silently erodes per-share value: 15% revenue growth against 7% dilution is a very different investment from 15% against 0%. Watch the trend, not the level.
metrics.usage:
Watch the trend; the level tells you nothing on its own.

Rising 5-8% a year roughly halves your ownership over a decade. That is why 15% revenue growth against 7% dilution is a completely different investment from 15% against zero — the second grows your slice, the first barely does.

Falling means buybacks, which only create value when done below intrinsic value. Many companies buy back hardest at the top.

metrics.label: SBC % of Revenue
metrics.description: Stock-based compensation as a share of revenue. The real cost behind dilution.
metrics.usage:
The cost behind the dilution above, and a real expense however the company presents its adjusted numbers.

Above roughly 10% of revenue is heavy. Compare within the group rather than across — norms differ enormously between software and hardware.

metrics.label: Net Debt/EBITDA
metrics.description: Leverage against cash generation. The number that decides whether a cyclical survives the trough.
metrics.usage:
The number that decides whether a cyclical survives its trough. Under 2x is comfortable; over 4x is fragile. Negative means net cash.

For a cyclical, judge it against TROUGH EBITDA rather than today's. Leverage that looks fine at the peak can be fatal when earnings halve — which is exactly when the multiple looked cheapest.

metrics.label: Interest Coverage
metrics.description: EBIT over interest expense. More predictive of distress than the debt level.
metrics.usage:
More predictive of distress than the debt level itself, because it asks whether the company can actually service what it owes.

Below about 3x leaves no room if earnings fall. Above 10x means debt is simply not an issue worth thinking about.

metrics.label: Capex % of Revenue
metrics.description: Capital intensity, and whether management is holding discipline through the cycle.
metrics.usage:
Capital intensity, and the main lever management controls in semis and energy.

A sharp rise is either a growth investment cycle or a treadmill. Check whether ROIC rises with it — if capex climbs and returns don't, the spending is maintaining the business rather than growing it.

metrics.label: Net Debt
metrics.description: Total debt less cash. Negative means net cash.
metrics.usage: Negative means net cash. Read it alongside Net Debt/EBITDA rather than alone — the absolute figure means little without the cash generation standing behind it.
